Neonatal scalloped hammerhead sharks emerge from their mothers following a gestation period that lasts approximately 305 days [ab = approximately 305 days] when water temperatures hover around 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. Upon parturition, these live-born pups measure roughly 49 cm [Lb = roughly 49 cm] in fork length, a value that aligns well with the range of 43 to 55 cm reported in arkive records for this species. This size at birth is modest relative to the formidable dimensions attained by adults and reflects the constraints of a placental viviparous reproductive mode in which embryonic growth depends on a limited maternal nutrient supply throughout gestation. The yolk-sac resorption that precedes parturition ensures that neonates are ready for independent foraging immediately after birth, yet they remain vulnerable to predation during their first year of life. Field surveys in nursery grounds such as Kaneohe Bay, Oahu, have documented that these young-of-the-year individuals often remain in shallow coastal waters where prey availability is high and predator encounter rates with large sharks are reduced. This early life stage is characterized by relatively rapid somatic growth, though the exact rates vary considerably with local thermal regimes and prey abundance.

Females of this species ultimately reach a maximum fork length of 241 cm [Li = 241 cm], while males attain a slightly smaller ultimate size of 234 cm [Li = 234 cm]. These asymptotic lengths are well below the theoretical maximum inferred from allometric scaling relationships but are consistent with mark-recapture studies conducted in the eastern Pacific. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females has been measured at 83820 grams [Wwi = 83820 grams], a body mass that is attained only after many years of sustained growth. Upon reaching sexual maturity, females experience a pronounced shift in energy allocation, with resources increasingly directed toward reproduction rather than continued somatic expansion. This trade-off is reflected in the comparatively modest weight gain observed in post-pubertal individuals. It is worth noting that the maximum total length occasionally reported in popular accounts, such as the 430 cm individual cited in some databases, would correspond to a much greater mass exceeding 152 kilograms, but such extreme sizes have not been verified in rigorous scientific surveys for Sphyrna lewini specifically.

The onset of reproductive maturity in scalloped hammerheads is marked by distinct size thresholds that differ markedly between the sexes. Females typically reach puberty at a fork length of 250 cm [Lp = 250 cm], a substantial size that reflects the considerable body volume required to support gestation of a large litter. Males, in contrast, become sexually mature at a much smaller size, reaching puberty at a fork length of 165 cm [Lp = 165 cm], indicating a less energetically demanding reproductive role. This sexual dimorphism in maturation size is common among carcharhiniform sharks and is thought to arise from the differential energetic costs imposed by pregnancy on females versus the comparatively low costs of spermatogenesis in males. At the onset of sexual maturation, females weigh approximately 80000 grams [Wwp = approximately 80000 grams], while males attain puberty at a wet weight of roughly 29000 grams [Wwp = roughly 29000 grams]. These weight-based thresholds provide an additional metric for assessing population maturity status in fisheries-independent surveys, complementing the more commonly reported length-based assessments.

The maximum daily reproduction rate in this species has been calculated to be approximately 20.1 pups per 365 days [Ri = approximately 20.1 pups per 365 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This rate, expressed as the total annual pup output per reproductively active female, is a consequence of both moderate litter sizes and a biennial or triennial reproductive cycle observed in many populations. Fecundity per reproductive event typically ranges from 15 to 31 pups, and females are capable of producing a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] under optimal environmental conditions. However, in cooler waters or during periods of prey scarcity, inter-birth intervals may lengthen substantially, reducing the effective annual reproductive output. The relatively low maximum reproductive rate compared to teleost fishes reflects the constraints of viviparity and the extended gestation period characteristic of this species. This life-history strategy, which emphasizes high offspring survival through large neonatal size rather than high fecundity, is typical of many large-bodied elasmobranchs.

Longevity data for scalloped hammerheads indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 35 years [am = approximately 35 years] when individuals are maintained under stable thermal conditions near 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This extended lifespan, in combination with late age at maturity and low natural mortality rates in adults, places Sphyrna lewini at the slow end of the elasmobranch life-history continuum. The species is particularly vulnerable to overexploitation because the combination of delayed maturation and protracted generation times means that population recovery from depletion is exceedingly slow. Age determination studies based on vertebral band counts have confirmed that individuals can persist for several decades in the wild, though fishing pressure has severely truncated the age structure in many regional populations. The biological death that eventually occurs in old individuals is typically the result of senescence-related physiological deterioration rather than predation, as fully grown adults have few natural enemies aside from killer whales and larger shark species. Conservation efforts must therefore account for these demographic attributes when setting sustainable harvest limits.
